title: Get command help
description: Display full documentation for any PowerShell cmdlet, including parameter details, examples, and notes.

The cmdlet to get help for

flags.description: Display full help including detailed parameter info and examples

output:
NAME
    Get-Process

SYNOPSIS
    Gets the processes that are running on the local computer.

EXAMPLE 1
    PS> Get-Process
    Lists all running processes with CPU and memory info.

EXAMPLE 2
    PS> Get-Process -Name notepad
    Gets only processes named notepad.
tip: Run 'Update-Help' once after installing PowerShell to download the latest help files. Use 'Get-Command *process*' to discover cmdlets matching a keyword.

title: Top CPU processes
description: List running processes sorted by CPU usage — the PowerShell equivalent of ps aux | sort. Returns objects with properties like CPU, WorkingSet, Id, and ProcessName.

breakdown.meaning: Retrieve all running processes with their stats
Pipe output to the next cmdlet

flags.description: Filter by process name (wildcards supported: *chrome*)
Get process by ID
Include the username of the process owner (requires elevation)

example: Get-Process -Name chrome | Select-Object Name, CPU, WorkingSet
tip: Pipe to 'Stop-Process' to kill matching processes: 'Get-Process -Name notepad | Stop-Process'. Use 'Get-Process | Out-GridView' for an interactive sortable table.

title: List running services
description: List Windows services and their current status (Running, Stopped, Paused) — use to audit running services or check whether a specific service is active.

breakdown.meaning: Retrieve all Windows services and their status
Pipe output to the next cmdlet

flags.description: Filter by service name (wildcards: *sql*)

example: Get-Service -Name wuauserv | Select-Object Name, Status, StartType
output:
Name     Status  StartType
----     ------  ---------
wuauserv Running Automatic
tip: Start/stop services with 'Start-Service wuauserv' and 'Stop-Service wuauserv' (requires admin). Use 'Set-Service -StartupType Disabled' to disable auto-start.

title: Query Windows Event Log
description: Retrieve recent error events from the Windows System event log — the primary tool for diagnosing Windows system issues.

breakdown.meaning: Read events from Windows event logs
Query the System log (also: Application, Security)

flags.description: Log name: System, Application, Security, or a custom log

Query event log on a remote computer

example: Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Application'; Level=2; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddHours(-24)} | Select-Object TimeCreated, ProviderName, Message -First 10
output:
TimeCreated          ProviderName       Message
-----------          ------------       -------
2025-03-15 09:15:02  MSSQLSERVER        SQL Server failed to start
2025-03-15 08:30:45  Application Error  Faulting application nginx.exe
tip: Use '-FilterHashtable' instead of piping to Where-Object — it filters at the source and is significantly faster on large logs. Level 1=Critical, 2=Error, 3=Warning, 4=Info.

command: Get-Process | Select-Object Name, CPU, WorkingSet | Export-Csv -Path .\processes.csv -NoTypeInformation
title: Export data to CSV
description: Select specific properties from pipeline objects and export them to a CSV file — useful for reporting and further analysis in Excel.

Get-Service | Select-Object Name, Status, StartType | Export-Csv -Path .\services.csv -NoTypeInformation
Import-Csv .\services.csv | Where-Object Status -eq Stopped
output:
Name       Status  StartType
----       ------  ---------
wuauserv   Stopped Automatic
BITS       Stopped Automatic
tip: Use 'Import-Csv' to read back the file as PowerShell objects. For JSON output, pipe to 'ConvertTo-Json | Out-File data.json' instead.

command: try { Get-Content C:\file.txt -ErrorAction Stop } catch { Write-Error "Failed: $_" }
title: Error handling with try/catch
description: Catch and handle errors in PowerShell scripts using try/catch blocks — prevents script termination on non-fatal errors and enables custom error responses.

breakdown.meaning: Execute the block and watch for terminating errors
Read the file — this is the operation that might fail
Convert non-terminating errors to terminating ones so catch fires
Execute this block if a terminating error occurs

flags.description: Promote cmdlet errors to terminating so they are caught by catch
Suppress all errors from a cmdlet
Optional block that always runs after try/catch, even on error
Access the error message string from the caught exception

example: try { Invoke-WebRequest https://api.example.com -ErrorAction Stop } catch [System.Net.WebException] { Write-Warning 'Network error' }
output: Failed: Cannot find path 'C:\file.txt' because it does not exist.
tip: PowerShell has two types of errors: terminating and non-terminating. Catch only intercepts terminating errors — add -ErrorAction Stop to any cmdlet that should be caught. Use $_.Exception to access the full exception object.

tip: For REST APIs, prefer Invoke-RestMethod over Invoke-WebRequest — it automatically parses JSON responses. For deeply nested JSON, increase the -Depth parameter of ConvertTo-Json (default is 2, which truncates nested objects).
